title: string_view and Fast Parsing
summary: Slice text without copying using std::string_view, avoid its lifetime trap, parse numbers with std::from_chars, and read a whole input fast.
intro: A feed handler or an order gateway spends much of its time turning bytes into fields: find the next delimiter, cut out the symbol, turn digits into a number. With `std::string`, `substr`, and `std::stoi`, every field is a copy, some are heap allocations, and every bad number is an exception. `std::string_view` and `std::from_chars` do the same work without copying, allocating, or throwing. This lesson builds a parser for FIX-style order messages with them, and reads its input fast.

steps.title: string_view: a window, not a copy
steps.body:
Take an order message in FIX style, `tag=value` fields separated by `|`. The references lesson named `std::string_view` as a cheap read-only view of text, and here is what that means. A `std::string_view` from `<string_view>` is a pointer to characters someone else owns, plus a length: 16 bytes, whatever it views. Making one copies nothing.

```cpp
const std::string msg = "35=D|55=AAPL|44=19275|38=100";
std::string_view view = msg;
std::string_view symbol = view.substr(8, 4);           // no copy
std::cout << symbol << ' ' << symbol.size() << '\n';  // AAPL 4
```

It has the read-only half of `std::string`: `size`, `empty`, `[]`, `find`, `rfind`, `substr`, `==`, and `<`, plus `remove_prefix(n)` and `remove_suffix(n)`, which shrink the window from either end. The difference that matters is `substr`: on a `std::string` it builds a new string, and on a view it makes a new pointer and length.

How much does the copy cost? A `std::string` keeps up to 15 chars inside the object, as the strings lesson showed (the *small string optimization*), so most FIX fields copy without a heap allocation. A client order id like `11=DESK7-20261122-000042` is 24 chars, though, and allocates on every copy. On a Mac, libc++'s `std::string` is 24 bytes and keeps up to 22 chars inline, so the cutoff moves, but that field still allocates there.

Take a `std::string_view` by value in functions that only read text. It accepts a `std::string`, a literal, or another view without a copy, while a `const std::string&` parameter given a literal first builds a temporary string. C++17's view has no `starts_with` (that's C++20), so compare `sv.substr(0, n) == prefix`.

example.title: Splitting a FIX message two ways
example.prompt: Split one order message into fields with std::string::substr and with std::string_view, counting heap allocations for each.
example.output:
string fields: 5, allocations 1
view fields: 5, allocations 0
35=D (4)
11=DESK7-20261122-000042 (24)
55=AAPL (7)
44=19275 (8)
38=100 (6)
sizeof: string 32, string_view 16
example.explanation:
The `operator new` at the top replaces the global one, so `g_allocs` counts every heap allocation, with `std::malloc` from `<cstdlib>` doing the real work. The lesson on allocations, later in the track, covers this counter in full. Splitting with `std::string::substr` made five new strings, and four of them fit in the 15-char buffer inside a `std::string`. The 24-char client order id didn't, and that's the one allocation. Splitting with views made the same five fields and allocated nothing: each is a pointer into `msg` and a length.

The view loop shows the usual way to walk a view: `find` the next `|`, take `substr(0, bar)` as the field, then `remove_prefix` past the bar. The last field has no bar after it, so `find` returns `npos`, `substr(0, npos)` takes the rest, and the loop stops. Both vectors were reserved up front, so their own buffers don't count.

practice.title: Split tick lines
practice.prompt:
Split comma-separated tick lines into views, without copying any field.

1. Write `std::vector<std::string_view> split(std::string_view line, char sep)` that returns every field between separators, using `find`, `substr`, and `remove_prefix`. Two separators in a row give an empty field.
2. For each input line, print the number of fields and a colon, then each field in square brackets after a space.

Input:

```text
34200000000150,AAPL,19270,19280,300,500
34200000000420,MSFT,41005,41010,,200
```

Expected output:

```text
6: [34200000000150] [AAPL] [19270] [19280] [300] [500]
6: [34200000000420] [MSFT] [41005] [41010] [] [200]
```
hints: Loop forever with `while (true)`: find the separator, push `line.substr(0, at)`, and stop when `at` is `npos`.
`substr(0, npos)` is the whole rest of the view, so the last field needs no special case.
After pushing a field, `line.remove_prefix(at + 1)` drops it and its separator.

steps.title: The lifetime trap

example.title: A view into a reused buffer
example.prompt: Keep a field from one message as a view and as a copy, receive the next message into the same buffer, and print both.
example.output:
first:  view AAPL, copy AAPL
second: view MSFT, copy AAPL
value_of 44: 41010, missing tag empty: 1
example.explanation:
`receive` copies each message into the one global buffer with `wire.copy(g_buffer, sizeof g_buffer)`, which copies up to 64 chars and returns how many, the way a network read fills the same memory again and again, then returns a view of the buffer. `symbol_view` points at bytes 8 to 11 of that buffer, and `symbol_copy` owns its own `AAPL`. When the second message lands, the copy still says `AAPL`, but the view now shows `MSFT`, because it never held the text, only where it was.

Nothing here is undefined, since the buffer is still alive, which makes it the most dangerous version: no sanitizer complains, and a strategy that kept the view would quietly trade the wrong symbol. `value_of` returns an empty view for a tag it can't find, so the caller can test `empty()`.

practice.title: Remember the last order
practice.prompt:
Make the remembered order own its text, so the next message can't change it.

1. `LastOrder` keeps views into the receive buffer, so after the second message it shows the second order. Change both members to `std::string`.
2. In `remember`, build each member with `std::string(...)` from the view `value_of` returns. A view never turns into a string silently.
3. Leave `main` as it is: it reads two messages, remembers the first, receives the second, and prints both orders.

Input:

```text
35=D|11=ORD-0001|55=AAPL|38=100
35=D|11=ORD-0002|55=MSFT|38=50
```

Expected output:

```text
last: AAPL ORD-0001
now: MSFT ORD-0002
```

tests.output:
last: AAPL ORD-0001
now: MSFT ORD-0002

last: NVDA A1
now: IBM LONGER-ID-77

last: SPY X-9
now: QQQ X-10

hints: Only `LastOrder` and `remember` change. `value_of` and `receive` are right as they are.
`LastOrder{value_of(msg, "55"), ...}` stops compiling once the members are strings: a view converts to a string only explicitly.

steps.title: std::from_chars: numbers without copies

example.title: Every outcome of from_chars, and prices in ticks
example.prompt: Show what std::from_chars does with good and bad tokens, then parse decimal prices into integer ticks of 0.01.
example.explanation:
`show` prints every outcome of one `from_chars` call. `"12abc"` parses 12 and stops at the `a`, so a parser that checks `ptr` sees the leftover text that `std::stoi` would have ignored. A leading space or `+` is no digit at all, and 20 nines don't fit in an `int64_t`.

`price_ticks` builds a decimal parser from two integer parses: the digits before the dot are dollars, and exactly two after it are cents. `to_uint` refuses a leading `-` itself, because `from_chars` into a signed type would take `"-0"` as 0 and let `-0.50` through as 50 ticks. `192.7` has one decimal, `19275` has no dot, and `1.2x` leaves text after the digits, so all three are refused rather than guessed at.

practice.title: FX prices in ticks
practice.prompt:
Parse FX prices into ticks of 0.00001 (a tenth of a pip).

1. Write `to_uint(s)`: an optional holding all of `s` as an integer, empty if `s` is empty, starts with `-`, or isn't a whole number. Use `std::from_chars` and check `ptr`.
2. Write `fx_ticks(s)`: up to 4 digits, a dot, then exactly 5 decimals. Return `whole * 100000 + decimals`, or an empty optional.
3. For each input token print `token -> ticks`, or `token -> invalid`.

Input:

```text
1.08345 0.65432 1.0834 7.24510 -1.00000 1.08x45
```

Expected output:

```text
1.08345 -> 108345
0.65432 -> 65432
1.0834 -> invalid
7.24510 -> 724510
-1.00000 -> invalid
1.08x45 -> invalid
```
hints: `to_uint` is the example's version, word for word.
Five decimals means `s.size() - dot == 6`, and up to 4 digits before the dot means `dot <= 4`.
An empty whole part, as in `.27410`, makes `to_uint` return an empty optional, so it's refused with no extra check.

steps.title: A zero-copy FIX parser and fast input
steps.body:
Now put the pieces together. A FIX message is a list of `tag=value` fields. Real FIX separates them with the byte 0x01 (SOH), which logs print as `|`, and these messages use `|`. `35=D|55=AAPL|44=19275|38=100` is a new order (`35=D`) for 100 (`38`) shares of AAPL (`55`) at 19275 ticks (`44`, sent as ticks in this lesson's messages).

The parser walks the message once. For each field it finds the `|`, splits at the `=`, turns the tag into an integer with `from_chars`, and acts on it. The symbol stays a view into the input, the numbers become integers, and nothing is copied or allocated. It returns `std::optional<NewOrder>`, empty for a malformed message, which is validating at the edge from the lesson on errors in fast code.

Fast input is the other half. `std::cin >> x` does real work on every call, and by default the C++ streams stay in sync with C's stdio, which costs on every read too. Two lines remove the syncing and the flushing, the first of them the one the user input lesson used, and reading all of stdin in one go then beats any per-number read. `std::ostringstream` is the writing twin of `std::istringstream`, and `<<` with `std::cin.rdbuf()` pours the whole input into it:

```stdin
35=D|55=AAPL|44=19275|38=100
35=D|55=MSFT|44=41010|38=50
```

```cpp
std::ios::sync_with_stdio(false);  // C++ streams stop syncing with C's stdio
std::cin.tie(nullptr);             // reads stop flushing std::cout first
std::ostringstream all;
all << std::cin.rdbuf();           // the whole input, in big blocks
const std::string input = all.str();
std::cout << input.size() << " bytes\n";  // 57 bytes
```

Views into `input` stay valid as long as `input` lives, which here is all of `main`. Timed in the sandbox on 500,000 numbers, `std::cin >> x` took about 90 ms, about 25 ms after the first two lines, and reading everything at once and parsing it with `from_chars` about 11 ms (2 to read, 9 to parse). Another common idiom, building a string from `std::istreambuf_iterator`, took 75 ms just to read, because it moves one char at a time. All these times are rough, since the sandbox runs x86-64 emulated.

example.title: New order messages from stdin
example.prompt: Read all of stdin at once, parse each FIX new order message into views and integers, and count the allocations.
example.output:
AAPL 100 @ 19275
MSFT 50 @ 41010
NVDA 200 @ 13950
rejected 2, allocations while parsing 0
example.explanation:
All of stdin arrives in one `std::string`, and from there everything is a view. `order->symbol` reads a member of the value inside the optional, like `->` on a pointer. The outer loop cuts lines with `find('\n')`, and `parse` cuts fields with `find('|')` and `find('=')`. The tag goes through `to_int`, so a field like `x=1` makes the whole message invalid instead of throwing from `std::stoi`. Tags the gateway doesn't use, like `11` and `54` in the second order, are skipped. `35=F` is a cancel, not a new order, and `44=13x50` isn't a whole number, so both count as rejected.

The replaced `operator new` at the top counts allocations again, and its count covers the whole loop, printing included: zero. Each `NewOrder` holds a view of its symbol, which is safe because `input` outlives every order printed here. An order that had to outlive the input would copy its symbol.

practice.title: Cancel requests
practice.prompt:
Parse FIX cancel requests with the same zero-copy approach.

1. Write `parse_cancel(msg)` returning `std::optional<CancelRequest>`. Tag `35` must be `F`. Keep tag `41` (the original order id) and tag `55` (the symbol) as views, and parse tag `38` (the quantity) with `to_int`. Skip any other tag.
2. Return an empty optional when a field has no `=`, a tag or the quantity isn't a whole number, `35` isn't `F`, the id or symbol is missing, or the quantity isn't above 0.
3. `main` reads the whole input and prints `cancel id symbol qty` for each good message, then `rejected N`.

Input:

```text
35=F|41=ORD-17|11=ORD-18|55=MSFT|38=50
35=D|55=AAPL|44=19275|38=100
35=F|41=ORD-3|55=NVDA|38=2x0
35=F|11=ORD-20|41=ORD-9|55=AAPL|38=100
```

Expected output:

```text
cancel ORD-17 MSFT 50
cancel ORD-9 AAPL 100
rejected 2
```

tests.output:
cancel ORD-17 MSFT 50
cancel ORD-9 AAPL 100
rejected 2

hints: Copy the example's `parse` loop and change the tags: `35` must be `"F"`, then `41`, `55`, and `38`.
A line without any `=`, like `bad message`, fails at the `eq == std::string_view::npos` check.
Check the id, the symbol, and the quantity after the loop, since the fields can come in any order.

recap:
- `std::string_view` is a pointer and a length, 16 bytes. Making one, `substr`, `remove_prefix`, and `remove_suffix` copy nothing.
- A `std::string` copy allocates only past its inline buffer: 15 chars with libstdc++, 22 with libc++ on a Mac. Views never allocate.
- Take `std::string_view` by value for read-only text. C++17 has no `starts_with`: compare `substr(0, n)`.
- A view dangles when its owner dies, grows, or moves, and g++ 10 doesn't warn. On a Mac, clang warns for many cases and `-fsanitize=address` catches the rest at run time.
- A view into a reused buffer silently shows the new contents. Copy what you keep with `std::string(view)`.
- `std::from_chars(first, last, value)` never allocates or throws: check `ec == std::errc{}` and `ptr == last`. It takes `-` for signed types, but no spaces or `+`.
- g++ 10 has `from_chars` for integers only, so parse prices as integer ticks: `"192.75"` becomes 19275.
- For big inputs: `std::ios::sync_with_stdio(false)`, `std::cin.tie(nullptr)`, then read it all with `all << std::cin.rdbuf()` and parse views into that one string.

That ends Modern C++ in Depth. Next, **Templates, Virtual Calls, std::function, and std::variant** opens the Performance section by putting the ways to pass behavior side by side, with their assembly and their allocations.
